notes.body:
The ruling turns on a principle that runs through all of Ismaili jurisprudence: **the weightier the obligation, the stricter its conditions.** Obligatory prayer (فرض) is what every worshipper owes Allah as an inescapable debt. Supererogatory prayer (نافلة) and the sunna are freely given acts of devotion beyond that minimum, held to a lighter standard.

A Prophetic saying bears directly on the question:

جُعِلَتْ لِي الْأَرْضُ مَسْجِدًا وَطَهُورًا
The earth has been made for me a place of prostration and a means of purification.

From this flows a precise ruling: **anything from which dry ablution (تيمم) cannot be performed is not a valid surface for prayer.** Dry ablution works by striking fine earth and drawing it across the face and hands as a substitute purification. Both stone and unbaked brick fall short of that standard:

- Stone is hard and yields no fine dust.
- Unbaked brick, though shaped from clay, has stiffened past that loose, purifying quality.

For voluntary prayers, the calculus shifts — not because the conditions are abandoned, but because the نافلة is a gift, not a debt. Think of how a formal contract requires precise language and witnesses, while a personal letter may be written on whatever paper is at hand — **the obligatory is the contract; the supererogatory is the letter.** Stone and unbaked brick, imperfect as they are, are close enough to earth to carry the voluntary prayer without invalidating it.
notes.anchor: Obligatory prayer upon them is not permitted; only the supererogatory…
notes.quote: Obligatory prayer upon them is not permitted; only the supererogatory and the sunna prayer.
etymology: فرض: from the root ف-ر-ض, meaning to cut, notch, or incise. Just as a notch carved into wood marks a fixed, irreversible point, a فرض is a duty cut into the law — binding and inescapable. The image of incision explains why an obligatory act admits no relaxation in its conditions.

نافلة: from the root ن-ف-ل, meaning to give something additional or beyond what is owed. The plural أنفال — extra gains — appears in the Quran. A نافلة is a prayer offered as a bonus beyond the required account, which is precisely why it carries lighter ritual conditions than the فرض.

تيمم: from the root ي-م-م, meaning to aim at or to intend toward something. Performing تيمم means purposefully turning to the earth as a substitute purifier when water is unavailable. The root's sense of deliberate direction reminds us that intention is woven into the very name of this act.

سجود: from the root س-ج-د, meaning to bow low or to incline toward the ground in complete submission. The word captures not a polite nod but a total lowering of the self — which is why the surface of prostration is guarded so carefully, and the forehead's resting place must be worthy.

notes.body:
The link Maulana Ali draws is not arbitrary — it is a convergence of moral memory and physical risk. The متوشح style, a shirt draped loosely across the body without being belted or properly fastened, was associated in the tradition with the people of Lot, a community whose identity in the Quran is inseparable from the **deliberate abandonment of shame**. When a man enters prayer wearing the mark of that association, he carries the spirit of that rejection into the most sacred moment of his day.

During bowing and prostrating, a loosely draped garment shifts unpredictably, and the private area (عورة) — the part of the body that must remain covered for prayer to be valid — can be exposed. Even a single thick shirt is permitted in prayer, but only if the worshipper belts it securely; every movement of prayer must leave **nothing exposed**. The متوشح style cannot guarantee that, and so it fails the prayer's most basic condition.

Prayer is an audience before Allah. Every detail of how we present ourselves — what we wear, how we wear it, what associations we carry — matters because the One we are standing before is not indifferent to such things. The people of Lot are remembered precisely for their indifference to the limits Allah set; to dress like them in prayer is to **echo that indifference** at the worst possible moment.

Maulana Ali's counsel closes the circle: let none of you stand before Allah, the Mighty and Exalted, except in a **clean garment**. Clean encompasses more than freedom from physical impurity; it means the garment carries no associations that diminish the holiness of the moment.

notes.quote: A man is not to pray in a shirt draped loosely across him, for that is the practice of the people of Lot.
etymology: متوشح (draped loosely across the body): from the root و-ش-ح, which describes crossing something diagonally over a surface — like a sash worn across the chest. The derived verb تَوَشَّحَ means to drape a garment over oneself in this crossing manner without fastening it. The root captures the instability of the style: placed across, not secured.

عورة (private area, that which must be covered): from the root ع-و-ر, which conveys a defect, a gap, or an exposed vulnerability — seen also in أَعْوَر, meaning one-eyed or impaired in one eye. The عورة is literally the 'vulnerable point': that which, left uncovered, opens a gap in the prayer's legal and spiritual validity.
